claim: Robust sleep/wake rhythms are important for health and cognitive function.
source: Robust sleep/wake rhythms are important for health and cognitive function.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about circadian rhythms and health.

claim: Many people are living in an environment where their circadian system is challenged by inappropriate meal- or work-times.
source: Unfortunately, many people are living in an environment where their circadian system is challenged by inappropriate meal- or work-times.
evidence: This is a general observation about modern society that is commonly known and referenced in circadian research.

claim: Scheduling food access to the sleep time does not alter the molecular clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).
source: Under these conditions, we demonstrate that the molecular clock in the master pacemaker, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), is unaltered while the molecular clock in the hippocampus is synchronized by the timing of food availability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PER2::LUC bioluminescence measurements showing no phase shift in SCN.

claim: The molecular clock in the hippocampus is synchronized by the timing of food availability.
source: Under these conditions, we demonstrate that the molecular clock in the master pacemaker, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), is unaltered while the molecular clock in the hippocampus is synchronized by the timing of food availability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PER2::LUC bioluminescence measurements showing phase shift in hippocampus.

claim: Chronic circadian misalignment causes reduced hippocampal long term potentiation.
source: This chronic circadian misalignment causes reduced hippocampal long term potentiation and total CREB expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing reduced LTP in misaligned mice.

claim: Chronic circadian misalignment causes reduced total CREB expression.
source: This chronic circadian misalignment causes reduced hippocampal long term potentiation and total CREB expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing decreased tCREB levels in misaligned mice.

claim: Mis-timed feeding resulted in dramatic deficits in hippocampal-dependent learning and memory.
source: Importantly this mis-timed feeding resulted in dramatic deficits in hippocampal-dependent learning and memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from fear conditioning and novel object recognition tests.

claim: The timing of meals have far-reaching effects on hippocampal physiology and learned behaviour.
source: Our findings suggest that the timing of meals have far-reaching effects on hippocampal physiology and learned behaviour.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: The circadian system is a finely tuned network of central and peripheral oscillators headed by a master pacemaker, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).
source: The circadian system is a finely tuned network of central and peripheral oscillators headed by a master pacemaker, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), which governs daily rhythms in physiology and behaviour, including cognition.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the circadian system organization.

claim: The circadian network regulates cognitive processes.
source: This network regulates cognitive processes (Holloway and Wansley, 1973; Chaudhury and Colwell, 2002), and the neural circuits involved in learning and memory also exhibit circadian rhythms in gene expression and synaptic plasticity (Eckel-Mahan et al., 2008; Fropf et al., 2014; Lamont et al., 2005; Lyons, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Neural circuits involved in learning and memory exhibit circadian rhythms in gene expression and synaptic plasticity.
source: This network regulates cognitive processes (Holloway and Wansley, 1973; Chaudhury and Colwell, 2002), and the neural circuits involved in learning and memory also exhibit circadian rhythms in gene expression and synaptic plasticity (Eckel-Mahan et al., 2008; Fropf et al., 2014; Lamont et al., 2005; Lyons, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Genetic disruption of molecular oscillations has severe consequences on cognition.
source: Genetic disruption of these molecular oscillations has severe consequences on cognition (Van der Zee et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2009; Wardlaw et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Environmental perturbations have the capacity to disrupt synchrony and misalign the clock network.
source: Environmental perturbations also have the capacity to disrupt synchrony and misalign this clock network (Fekete et al., 1985; Cho et al., 2000; Devan et al., 2001; Ruby et al., 2008; Loh et al., 2010; Gibson et al., 2010; Karatsoreos et al., 2011; Fonken et al., 2012; LeGates et al., 2012; Fernandez et al., 2014) and are problematic as many people in our modern society extend their work and recreation into the night hours.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The timing of when we eat is critical for our metabolic health.
source: There has been mounting evidence that the timing of when we eat is critical for our metabolic health (Bass, 2012; Mattson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Timing of food intake has a major impact on the phase of the molecular oscillations in peripheral organs such as the liver and pancreas.
source: At this point, timing of food intake is well-established to have a major impact on the phase of the molecular oscillations in peripheral organs such as the liver and pancreas (Damiola, 2000; Stokkan, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Mis-timed meals during the sleep phase accelerates weight gain compared with animals fed during their wake phase.
source: Mis-timed meals during the sleep phase accelerates weight gain compared with animals fed during their wake phase (Arble et al., 2009; Bray et al., 2013), whereas wake-phase feeding has a protective effect against the cardiac and metabolic dysfunction caused by high fat diets (Hatori et al., 2012; Gill et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Wake-phase feeding has a protective effect against the cardiac and metabolic dysfunction caused by high fat diets.
source: Mis-timed meals during the sleep phase accelerates weight gain compared with animals fed during their wake phase (Arble et al., 2009; Bray et al., 2013), whereas wake-phase feeding has a protective effect against the cardiac and metabolic dysfunction caused by high fat diets (Hatori et al., 2012; Gill et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Misaligned mealtimes in humans produce cardiac and metabolic deficits, leading to a pre-diabetic state.
source: Similar disruptive effects are seen in humans, where misaligned mealtimes produce cardiac and metabolic deficits, leading to a pre-diabetic state (Scheer et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous research study.

claim: Mice adapted to the feeding protocol within 6 days.
source: Mice adapted to the feeding protocol within 6 days (p = 0.9, Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on food consumption showing no difference by day 6.

claim: There were no significant differences in body weight between aligned and misaligned groups at the time of testing.
source: there were no significant differences in body weight between the two groups at the time of testing (p = 0.5, Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on body weight measurements.

claim: Daytime activity was increased in mice subjected to misaligned feeding.
source: Daytime activity was increased in mice subjected to misaligned feeding (p < 0.001; Figure 3A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from activity monitoring.

claim: The strength of daily rhythms of activity was reduced by misaligned feeding.
source: the strength of daily rhythms of activity was reduced by misaligned feeding (p = 0.003; Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from chi-square periodogram analysis.

claim: The temporal pattern of sleep was altered by misaligned feeding.
source: Similarly, the temporal pattern of sleep was altered by misaligned feeding (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: Misaligned mice showed decreased time spent asleep during the day.
source: Immobility-defined video monitoring of sleep behaviour of misaligned mice showed decreased time spent asleep during the day (p < 0.001) and a corresponding increase in sleep during the night (p < 0.001; Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: Misaligned mice showed a corresponding increase in sleep during the night.
source: Immobility-defined video monitoring of sleep behaviour of misaligned mice showed decreased time spent asleep during the day (p < 0.001) and a corresponding increase in sleep during the night (p < 0.001; Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: Misaligned mice no longer exhibit a day vs night difference in sleep, sleeping equally during the day and night.
source: Misaligned mice no longer exhibit a day vs night difference in sleep, sleeping equally during the day and night (p = 0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: The total time spent asleep over a 24 hr day was not reduced by misaligned feeding.
source: Crucially, the total time spent asleep over a 24 hr day was not reduced by misaligned feeding (p = 0.2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: Misaligned mice exhibit a greater number of sleep bouts during the day compared to aligned mice.
source: The change in temporal pattern of sleep quantity is also reflected in sleep fragmentation, where misaligned mice exhibit a greater number of sleep bouts (p < 0.05) with a corresponding decrease in average sleep bout duration (p < 0.001) during the day compared to aligned mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: Misaligned mice exhibit a corresponding decrease in average sleep bout duration during the day compared to aligned mice.
source: The change in temporal pattern of sleep quantity is also reflected in sleep fragmentation, where misaligned mice exhibit a greater number of sleep bouts (p < 0.05) with a corresponding decrease in average sleep bout duration (p < 0.001) during the day compared to aligned mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: Increased day-time sleep fragmentation in misaligned mice is compensated by fewer and longer night sleep bouts.
source: This increased day-time sleep fragmentation is compensated by fewer (p < 0.05) and longer (p < 0.001) night sleep bouts in the misaligned animals, resulting in no significant change in the total number (p = 0.9) and average duration (p = 0.6) of sleep bouts over a 24 hr period.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: There is no significant change in the total number of sleep bouts over a 24 hr period in misaligned mice.
source: This increased day-time sleep fragmentation is compensated by fewer (p < 0.05) and longer (p < 0.001) night sleep bouts in the misaligned animals, resulting in no significant change in the total number (p = 0.9) and average duration (p = 0.6) of sleep bouts over a 24 hr period.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: There is no significant change in the average duration of sleep bouts over a 24 hr period in misaligned mice.
source: This increased day-time sleep fragmentation is compensated by fewer (p < 0.05) and longer (p < 0.001) night sleep bouts in the misaligned animals, resulting in no significant change in the total number (p = 0.9) and average duration (p = 0.6) of sleep bouts over a 24 hr period.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: Daytime feeding shifts the phase of the liver oscillator without altering the phase of the SCN oscillator.
source: Using ex vivo organotypic cultures of explants from PER2::LUC reporter mice subjected to aligned or misaligned feeding, we confirmed that daytime feeding shifts the phase of the liver oscillator (p < 0.001) without altering the phase of the SCN oscillator (p = 0.07; Figure 4A,C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PER2::LUC bioluminescence measurements.

claim: Daytime feeding significantly misaligns the hippocampal oscillator by 14.1 hr.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate that daytime feeding significantly misaligns the hippocampal oscillator by 14.1 hr (p < 0.001; Figure 4B,D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PER2::LUC bioluminescence measurements.

claim: Daytime feeding has small but significant effects on the period of the hippocampal oscillator.
source: with small but significant effects on the intrinsic properties of the oscillator, including period (p = 0.05; Figure 4E) and damping rate (p = 0.02; Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PER2::LUC bioluminescence measurements.

claim: Daytime feeding has small but significant effects on the damping rate of the hippocampal oscillator.
source: with small but significant effects on the intrinsic properties of the oscillator, including period (p = 0.05; Figure 4E) and damping rate (p = 0.02; Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PER2::LUC bioluminescence measurements.

claim: Expression of tCREB was significantly reduced by misaligned feeding.
source: Strikingly, expression of tCREB was significantly reduced by misaligned feeding (p < 0.01; Figure 5A,C,D), with the strongest effects in the day (post hoc p < 0.05 for ZT 2, 8, and 20).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis.

claim: The decrease in tCREB levels was uniformly observed throughout the hippocampus.
source: This decrease in tCREB levels was uniformly observed throughout the hippocampus (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry.

claim: LTP was significantly impaired in the misaligned group.
source: LTP was significantly impaired in the misaligned group (p< 0.05; Figure 5E), indicating significant deficits in synaptic plasticity in the misaligned hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The decrease in LTP is specific to the misaligned feeding treatment and not due to an LTP-boosting effect by aligned feeding.
source: This decrease in LTP is specific to the misaligned feeding treatment and not due to an LTP-boosting effect by aligned feeding (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing misaligned mice to ad libitum controls.

claim: There were no significant differences between the aligned and misaligned paired pulse facilitation ratios.
source: There were no significant differences between the aligned and misaligned PPF ratios (p = 0.5; Figure 5F), and EPSP profiles were similar.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from paired pulse facilitation experiments.

claim: Both aligned and misaligned mice acquired freezing behaviour during the training trial.
source: Both aligned and misaligned mice acquired freezing behaviour during the training trial (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning training.

claim: Misaligned mice exhibited a significant reduction in fear-conditioned behaviour when tested 24 hr later during the day.
source: When tested 24 hr later by replacing the mice in the same context, the misaligned mice exhibited a significant reduction in fear-conditioned behaviour (ZT 2, p < 0.0001; Figure 6A, left), indicating that circadian misalignment affects long term memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning recall tests.

claim: Performance on the fear conditioning test is dependent on time of day and performance peaks in the early day.
source: Performance on the fear conditioning test is dependent on time of day and performance peaks in the early day (Chaudhury and Colwell, 2002; Eckel-Mahan et al., 2008; Loh et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Night-tested aligned and misaligned mice exhibited equally poor recall.
source: Night-tested aligned and misaligned mice exhibited equally poor recall (post hoc p = 0.4; Figure 6A, right), ruling out the possibility that the misaligned mice have an altered peak phase of cognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning recall tests at night.

claim: The misaligned mice exhibited significantly reduced novel object recognition during night-time tests.
source: The misaligned mice exhibited significantly reduced novel object recognition (NOR) during night-time tests (ZT 21, p < 0.001; Figure 6B, right), indicating decreased cognitive performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from novel object recognition tests.

claim: Aligned mice showed reduced NOR during the day.
source: Specifically, aligned mice showed reduced NOR during the day (post hoc p = 0.04), and day-tested misaligned mice were not significantly different from aligned (post hoc p = 0.6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from novel object recognition tests.

claim: Time-restricted feeding led to dramatic impairments in learned behaviours such as hippocampal-dependent contextual fear conditioning and novel object recognition.
source: We found that time-restricted feeding led to dramatic impairments in learned behaviours such as hippocampal-dependent contextual fear conditioning and novel object recognition.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings from behavioral tests.

claim: Amygdala-dependent cued-fear conditioning was not altered by the misalignment.
source: Not all behavioural tests were similarly affected, as amygdala-dependent cued-fear conditioning was not altered by the misalignment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cued fear conditioning tests.

claim: Some learned behaviours are more vulnerable to the impact of misaligned feeding.
source: This implies that some learned behaviours are more vulnerable to the impact of misaligned feeding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects on different behavioral tests.

claim: The total amount of sleep was not altered by the scheduled feeding.
source: Crucially, the total amount of sleep was not altered by the scheduled feeding and the mice did not lose weight as might be expected if their caloric intake was restricted.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from sleep monitoring and body weight measurements.

claim: The mice did not lose weight as might be expected if their caloric intake was restricted.
source: Crucially, the total amount of sleep was not altered by the scheduled feeding and the mice did not lose weight as might be expected if their caloric intake was restricted.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from body weight measurements.

claim: By simply adjusting the time of food access, we can alter the cognitive performance of mice.
source: Hence, by simply adjusting the time of food access, we demonstrated that we can alter the cognitive performance of mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Shift work has been associated with decreased performance on cognitive tests.
source: We do not know yet if this equally applies to humans but shift work has been associated with decreased performance on cognitive tests (Wright et al., 2006; Marquie et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies on shift work in humans.

claim: The importance of sleep for memory is well-documented.
source: The importance of sleep for memory is well-documented, where both the amount of sleep and the quality of sleep have been found to be critical for memory consolidation (reviewed in Diekelmann and Born, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Both the amount of sleep and the quality of sleep have been found to be critical for memory consolidation.
source: The importance of sleep for memory is well-documented, where both the amount of sleep and the quality of sleep have been found to be critical for memory consolidation (reviewed in Diekelmann and Born, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The misaligned feeding treatment had a severe impact on the temporal pattern of sleep.
source: The misaligned feeding treatment did not result in an overall decrease in amount of sleep, but instead had a severe impact on the temporal pattern, suggesting that this treatment acts via disruption of the circadian timing of sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from sleep monitoring showing altered day/night distribution.

claim: The misaligned feeding treatment acts via disruption of the circadian timing of sleep.
source: The misaligned feeding treatment did not result in an overall decrease in amount of sleep, but instead had a severe impact on the temporal pattern, suggesting that this treatment acts via disruption of the circadian timing of sleep.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that total sleep is unchanged but temporal pattern is altered.

claim: Misaligned feeding has a greater impact on the temporal pattern of sleep fragmentation.
source: Misaligned feeding again has a greater impact on the temporal pattern of sleep fragmentation, where the misaligned mice appear to "catch up" on consolidated sleep during what should be their active phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on sleep bout number and duration.

claim: The altered feeding time shifted the peripheral clocks in the liver.
source: Mechanistically, we used the clock-driven rhythms in bioluminescence to demonstrate that the altered feeding time not only shifted the peripheral clocks in the liver, but also altered the circadian clock in the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PER2::LUC bioluminescence measurements.

claim: The altered feeding time altered the circadian clock in the hippocampus.
source: Mechanistically, we used the clock-driven rhythms in bioluminescence to demonstrate that the altered feeding time not only shifted the peripheral clocks in the liver, but also altered the circadian clock in the hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PER2::LUC bioluminescence measurements.

claim: The phasing of the molecular clock in the corticolimbic system and hippocampus are strongly influenced by the time of food availability.
source: This finding is consistent with earlier literature suggesting the phasing of the molecular clock in the corticolimbic system and hippocampus are strongly influenced by the time of food availability (Amir, 2004; Ángeles-Castellanos et al., 2007; Wakamatsu et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The manipulation created a situation in which the molecular clocks within the nervous system are running at different phases.
source: We have thus created a situation in which the molecular clocks within the nervous system are running at different phases, i.e. internal desynchronisation of the circadian system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that SCN and hippocampus have different phases.

claim: A consequence of this misalignment is altered synaptic plasticity within the hippocampal circuit as revealed by the reduction in LTP.
source: A consequence of this misalignment is altered synaptic plasticity within the hippocampal circuit (Schaffer Collaterals/CA1) as revealed by the reduction in LTP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from LTP recordings.

claim: This is the first demonstration that the time of eating can impact the physiological underpinning of learned behaviour.
source: This is the first demonstration that the time of eating can impact the physiological underpinning of learned behaviour.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The manipulation of feeding caused a significant decline in CREB in the hippocampus.
source: Importantly, our manipulation of feeding caused a significant decline in CREB in the hippocampus, which has been demonstrated to be critical for memory allocation in mice (e.g. Sano et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis.

claim: CREB has been demonstrated to be critical for memory allocation in mice.
source: Importantly, our manipulation of feeding caused a significant decline in CREB in the hippocampus, which has been demonstrated to be critical for memory allocation in mice (e.g. Sano et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The levels of tCREB were reduced at all phases sampled (ZT 2, 8, 14 and 20).
source: The levels of tCREB were reduced at all phases that we sampled (ZT 2, 8, 14 and 20), and although we did not carry out cognitive tests at each of these phases, this finding indicates that memory would be impaired throughout the daily cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis at multiple time points.

claim: Memory would be impaired throughout the daily cycle in misaligned mice.
source: The levels of tCREB were reduced at all phases that we sampled (ZT 2, 8, 14 and 20), and although we did not carry out cognitive tests at each of these phases, this finding indicates that memory would be impaired throughout the daily cycle.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that tCREB is reduced at all time points sampled.

claim: The reduction in tCREB provides a biochemical explanation for the memory impairment findings.
source: The reduction in tCREB provides a biochemical explanation for our finding, as well as providing a guidepost for future analysis of the effects of the misaligned feeding in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the biochemical finding to the behavioral outcomes.

claim: The timing of when we eat alters the physiological and biochemical events underlying learning and memory.
source: Therefore, this work raises the possibility that the timing of when we eat alters the physiological and biochemical events underlying learning and memory.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: pCREB protein levels were reduced in the misaligned animals at each time point, although significant differences were not detected.
source: pCREB protein levels were reduced in the misaligned animals at each time point, although significant differences were not detected (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis showing a trend but no statistical significance.

claim: Levels of β-actin do not vary with time of day in either group.
source: We confirmed by two way ANOVA comparisons that levels of β-actin do not vary with time of day in either group (p = 0.9) and is no different between aligned and misaligned mice (p = 0.9; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis of the loading control.

claim: β-actin levels are no different between aligned and misaligned mice.
source: We confirmed by two way ANOVA comparisons that levels of β-actin do not vary with time of day in either group (p = 0.9) and is no different between aligned and misaligned mice (p = 0.9; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Western blot analysis of the loading control.

claim: Misaligned mice caught up with aligned mice in daily food consumption by day 6 of scheduled feeding.
source: (a) Misaligned mice caught up with aligned mice in daily food consumption by day 6 of scheduled feeding (p = 0.9) and did not differ in food consumption subsequently (day 6–14 post hoc p > 0.2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on food consumption measurements.

claim: Misaligned mice did not differ in food consumption from aligned mice after day 6.
source: (a) Misaligned mice caught up with aligned mice in daily food consumption by day 6 of scheduled feeding (p = 0.9) and did not differ in food consumption subsequently (day 6–14 post hoc p > 0.2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on food consumption measurements.

claim: Body weights between treatment groups did not differ significantly through the duration of scheduled feeding.
source: (b) Mice were weighed daily prior to food access. Body weights between treatment groups did not differ significantly through the duration of scheduled feeding (two way ANOVA p = 0.3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on body weight measurements.

claim: Nocturnality (% activity in the night) is reduced in misaligned mice.
source: (b) Nocturnality (% activity in the night) is reduced in misaligned mice (***p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from activity monitoring.

claim: Rhythm strength measured by the amplitude of a chi-square periodogram (%V) is reduced in misaligned mice.
source: (c) Rhythm strength measured by the amplitude of a chi-square periodogram (%V) is reduced in misaligned mice (**p < 0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from activity monitoring.

claim: The number of sleep bouts during the day is increased in misaligned mice.
source: (a) The number of sleep bouts during the day is increased in misaligned mice, decreased at night, and unchanged between groups when considered over 24 hr (total).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: The number of sleep bouts at night is decreased in misaligned mice.
source: (a) The number of sleep bouts during the day is increased in misaligned mice, decreased at night, and unchanged between groups when considered over 24 hr (total).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: The number of sleep bouts over 24 hr is unchanged between groups.
source: (a) The number of sleep bouts during the day is increased in misaligned mice, decreased at night, and unchanged between groups when considered over 24 hr (total).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: The average duration of a sleep bout is shorter in misaligned mice during the day.
source: (b) The average duration of a sleep bout is shorter in misaligned mice during the day, longer at night, and unchanged between groups over 24 hr (total).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: The average duration of a sleep bout is longer in misaligned mice at night.
source: (b) The average duration of a sleep bout is shorter in misaligned mice during the day, longer at night, and unchanged between groups over 24 hr (total).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: The average duration of a sleep bout over 24 hr is unchanged between groups.
source: (b) The average duration of a sleep bout is shorter in misaligned mice during the day, longer at night, and unchanged between groups over 24 hr (total).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: The distribution of sleep bout lengths is similar between groups.
source: (c,d) The distribution of sleep bout lengths is similar between groups (p = 0.3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from video monitoring of sleep behavior.

claim: Misaligned mice did not show significant changes in baseline freezing.
source: (a) Misaligned mice did not show significant changes in baseline freezing (p = 0.3), freezing in response to the first foot shock (US-1; p = 0.9), or freezing in response to the second foot shock (US-2; p = 0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning training.

claim: Misaligned mice did not show significant changes in freezing in response to the first foot shock.
source: (a) Misaligned mice did not show significant changes in baseline freezing (p = 0.3), freezing in response to the first foot shock (US-1; p = 0.9), or freezing in response to the second foot shock (US-2; p = 0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning training.

claim: Misaligned mice did not show significant changes in freezing in response to the second foot shock.
source: (a) Misaligned mice did not show significant changes in baseline freezing (p = 0.3), freezing in response to the first foot shock (US-1; p = 0.9), or freezing in response to the second foot shock (US-2; p = 0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning training.

claim: Misaligned feeding did not cause differences in baseline freezing at night.
source: (b) Misaligned feeding did not cause differences in baseline freezing (p = 1.0), nor in acquisition of freezing in response to US-1 (p = 0.9) and US-2 (p = 0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning training at night.

claim: Misaligned feeding did not cause differences in acquisition of freezing in response to US-1 at night.
source: (b) Misaligned feeding did not cause differences in baseline freezing (p = 1.0), nor in acquisition of freezing in response to US-1 (p = 0.9) and US-2 (p = 0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning training at night.

claim: Misaligned feeding did not cause differences in acquisition of freezing in response to US-2 at night.
source: (b) Misaligned feeding did not cause differences in baseline freezing (p = 1.0), nor in acquisition of freezing in response to US-1 (p = 0.9) and US-2 (p = 0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning training at night.

claim: There was a time of day effect on freezing in response to US-2.
source: There was a time of day effect on freezing in response to US-2 (#p < 0.05), as previously reported (2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning training at different times of day.

claim: Two way comparisons revealed a time of day effect on recall.
source: Two way comparisons revealed a time of day effect on recall (p < 0.001) and an interaction between time of day and feeding condition (p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fear conditioning recall data.

claim: Two way comparisons revealed an interaction between time of day and feeding condition on recall.
source: Two way comparisons revealed a time of day effect on recall (p < 0.001) and an interaction between time of day and feeding condition (p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fear conditioning recall data.

claim: Recall was significantly reduced in the aligned mice compared to the daytime tests.
source: Recall was significantly reduced in the aligned mice compared to the daytime tests (post hoc p < 0.001), but did not significantly change with time of day in misaligned mice (post hoc p = 0.3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning recall tests at different times of day.

claim: Recall did not significantly change with time of day in misaligned mice.
source: Recall was significantly reduced in the aligned mice compared to the daytime tests (post hoc p < 0.001), but did not significantly change with time of day in misaligned mice (post hoc p = 0.3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning recall tests at different times of day.
